title: Hash Aggregate Spills From a Bad Estimate
description: The same 1-row table-variable estimate starves a Hash Aggregate and spills it; an indexed #temp lets the engine stream the aggregate. Why it matters: the same table-variable trap applies to GROUP BY, not just sorting -- recognizing the pattern once means catching it everywhere it appears.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is a close sibling of the table-variable-and-Sort problem covered elsewhere in this course — same root cause, different operator. It's worth learning both, because once you recognize the underlying pattern, you'll spot it anywhere it shows up in a plan, not just in the one specific place you first learned it.

When you write a `GROUP BY` on data that isn't already sorted by the grouping column, SQL Server needs some way to collect 'all the rows for group A' together, 'all the rows for group B' together, and so on, so it can count or sum each group. The classic way it does this is a **Hash Match (Aggregate)**: it builds an in-memory hash table — think of it like a set of labeled buckets, one per distinct group key — and as each row streams in, it computes a quick hash of the group key to figure out which bucket that row belongs to, drops it in, and updates a running count/sum for that bucket. Once every row has been processed, it walks the buckets and outputs one summary row per group. This is fast and effective, *as long as all those buckets fit comfortably in the memory SQL Server reserved for the operation.*

And just like with sorting, before the query even starts running, SQL Server has to decide up front how much memory to reserve for this hash table — a **memory grant** — and it bases that decision on its **cardinality estimate**: its prediction of how many rows (and therefore, roughly, how many distinct groups) it expects to see. This is exactly where the same trap as the Sort lesson reappears: a **table variable** (declared with `DECLARE @T TABLE (...)`), under many configurations, doesn't carry real statistics the way a normal table does — the optimizer simply assumes it holds **one row**, no matter how much data you've actually loaded into it. So if you load, say, 200,000 rows into a table variable, spread across roughly 50,000 distinct grouping values, and then run a `GROUP BY` on it, SQL Server plans the whole operation as if there's a single row and a single group to deal with. The Hash Match gets a memory grant sized for practically nothing.

Then reality hits: at execution time, 50,000 real buckets need to exist, each needing to track its own running count, and the tiny reserved memory simply can't hold them all. Just like the Sort operator in the sibling lesson, the Hash Match doesn't fail outright — it adapts by **spilling to tempdb**: it writes partial hash-table data out to disk, processes it in smaller batches that do fit in the available memory, and reads it back to merge and finish the aggregation. This shows up in the execution plan as a **Hash Match (Aggregate)** operator carrying a `SpillToTempDb` warning (the same yellow warning triangle you'd see on a spilling Sort). What should have been a fast, cheap, entirely-in-memory tally — counting 50,000 groups is genuinely trivial work for modern hardware — turns into repeated disk writes and reads, because the plan was built around a guess of 'one row' instead of the actual 200,000.

Why does the exact same mistake show up in two different places (Sort and Hash Match)? Because both operators share the identical dependency: they both need to reserve memory ahead of time based on a cardinality estimate, and a table variable feeds both of them the same wrong number. This is really the core insight worth internalizing — it's not 'table variables are bad at sorting' or 'table variables are bad at grouping' as two separate facts to memorize, it's one single fact: table variables (in this configuration) give the optimizer a fictional row count, and *any* memory-grant-dependent operator built on top of that estimate — Sort, Hash Match, Hash Join, and others — inherits the same bad assumption and is equally exposed to spilling once the real data volume grows past what a '1 row' guess would need.

The fix mirrors the Sort lesson too, with one extra twist specific to grouping: swap the table variable for a real **temporary table** (`#temp`), which carries genuine statistics so the memory grant gets sized for the real 50,000-group workload. But there's an even better option available specifically for `GROUP BY`: if you build the `#temp` table with a **clustered index on the grouping column**, the rows arrive at the aggregate step *already sorted* by that column. When input arrives pre-sorted by the grouping key, SQL Server doesn't need a hash table at all — it can use a **Stream Aggregate** instead, which simply walks the sorted rows in one pass, noticing when the group key changes and emitting a finished summary row for the group that just ended, before moving on to the next. A Stream Aggregate needs almost no extra memory and has nothing to spill, because it never builds a hash table in the first place — it just counts as it streams past, in order. Recognizing this one pattern — 'table variable feeding something that needs a cardinality-dependent memory grant' — is the transferable skill: once you've seen it break a Sort, you'll immediately recognize the identical shape when it breaks a Hash Match, a Hash Join, or anything else that sizes its workspace off the optimizer's row estimate.

## Scenario
A rollup loads rows into a **table variable** and then groups them to count per key. With ~50,000 groups it drags and pounds tempdb, even though the aggregation itself is trivial.

## Why it's slow
To `GROUP BY` an unordered set, SQL Server builds a **Hash Match (Aggregate)** — a hash table of all the group keys — and sizes its **memory grant** from the estimated row count. A **table variable** is estimated at **1 row**, so the aggregate is granted almost no memory. At run time it must hold 50,000 groups, overflows the grant, and **spills to tempdb** (`SpillToTempDb` on the Hash Match), turning an in-memory aggregation into repeated disk I/O.

## What to look for
- A **Hash Match (Aggregate)** carrying a `SpillToTempDb` warning.
- Estimated rows = 1 while actual rows = 200,000 feeding the aggregate.

## The concept
Give the optimizer honest cardinality. Load into a **`#temp` table** (real statistics) instead of a table variable, and put a **clustered index on the grouping key**. Now the rows arrive already ordered by `G`, so the engine uses a **Stream Aggregate** — it counts each group as it passes, needs no hash table, and has nothing to spill. Ordered input turns grouping from a memory-hungry hash into a streaming count.
hints: The Hash Match (Aggregate) has a SpillToTempDb warning. Why would it get a tiny memory grant?
A table variable estimates 1 row, so the hash aggregate is sized for 1 group and spills when it really holds 50,000.

Load into a #temp table with a clustered index on the grouping column G. Ordered input lets the optimizer use a Stream Aggregate (no hash, no spill): CREATE TABLE #T (G INT NOT NULL, Pad CHAR(40) NOT NULL, INDEX CX CLUSTERED (G));
